analysis.one_liner: Requires for-profit colleges to get at least 15% of revenue from non-federal sources, counting GI Bill benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate education committee in February 2021 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, for-profit colleges must draw at least 10% of their revenue from sources other than federal student aid, but GI Bill benefits don't count as federal funds. This bill would raise that bar to 15% and count veterans' education benefits as federal money, with an exception for the Post-9/11 GI Bill housing stipend. The aim is to limit how much of a for-profit college's income comes straight from the federal government, so schools must stay financially viable on their own rather than living almost entirely off federal aid. It also requires an annual report to Congress on how much federal money each for-profit school takes in.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at for-profit colleges, especially veterans using GI Bill benefits who schools could otherwise court as a new source of federal dollars; and taxpayers, who currently foot the bill when federally funded schools enroll students who end up defaulting on their loans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: For-profit college students, veterans, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum share of revenue for-profit colleges must get from non-federal sources from 10% to 15%, so a school that lives almost entirely off federal aid loses its eligibility.

Counts GI Bill education benefits as federal funds (excluding the Post-9/11 housing stipend), closing the loophole that let schools target veterans' benefits as revenue without it counting against the limit.
Requires the Education Department to report annually to Congress how much of each for-profit college's revenue comes from federal education assistance, using audited financial statements.

Tightens what counts as revenue under the rule — for example, excluding the school's own loans and counting institutional scholarships only when funded from an outside, unaffiliated source — to prevent accounting games that made the old rule easy to satisfy.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges, many of which rely on federal student aid for the overwhelming majority of their revenue; some schools that could not meet the 15% threshold would lose access to federal aid and could close.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit colleges dependent on federal aid

drawbacks.text: Schools that lose federal-aid eligibility or close would strand current students mid-program, leaving some without credits, degrees, or an easy path to transfer.
Raising the threshold could shrink veterans' and low-income students' access to some career-training programs, since schools facing the stricter math may cut enrollment in those programs.
The bill applies only to for-profit institutions; nonprofit and public colleges that leave students with unpayable debt face no comparable revenue test under this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real: students and veterans were being recruited into programs that often left them with debt and weak job prospects, funded almost entirely by federal money. The costs fall on the schools and, at the margin, on students enrolled in programs that might close. A fair accounting favors the students and taxpayers, though the bill does nothing about quality problems at nonprofit and public colleges and offers no direct fix for students already enrolled.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate's education committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, vote, or floor action ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on February 23, 2021, with nine cosponsors, all Democrats or independents.
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The bill received no further action in the committee and never came to the Senate floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges dependent on federal student aid revenue, which avoided a stricter revenue test, and the status quo of federal dollars flowing to those schools continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the push for the stricter revenue rule on for-profit colleges.

for.name: 9 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat in committee for the entire Congress.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.role: Colleges funded primarily by federal student aid and veterans' benefits
against.what_they_did: Worked to keep the existing 90/10 revenue rule in place, lobbying against changes that would count GI Bill benefits as federal revenue.

sides.party_line_note: All ten original supporters were Democrats or independents; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic-led committee never moved it, so the bill had a partisan shape on both sides.

industries.note: These schools draw the large majority of their revenue from federal student aid, and the bill would raise the minimum non-federal share to 15% while counting veterans' benefits as federal money — a direct threat to schools that live off federal dollars, some of which would lose aid eligibility or close. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against students and taxpayers who bear the cost of defaults and poor program outcomes.

industries.industry: Post-9/11 GI Bill users (veterans as a revenue pool)
industries.note: Veterans currently count toward for-profit colleges' non-federal revenue under the old rule, which made them a target for aggressive recruiting. The bill would make veterans' benefits count as federal revenue (their housing stipend excluded), reducing that incentive — veterans would still be able to use their benefits, but schools would have less reason to court them purely for the accounting benefit.
